paragraphs: Rabbi Chiyya, without qualification: son of R. Abba (bar Acha; see there for the difficulty), Bar Salla.

(a) He is R. Chiyya the Great, also called Berabbi (see there) and R. Chiyya Rabbah. He descended from Shimi, David's brother: chapter Metziat HaIshah; chapter Af Al Pi, 62b. Yuchasin writes, under Hillel: it is puzzling why his daughter, betrothed to Rabbi's son, died (Af Al Pi, there). Was he not of better lineage? Rabbi descended from Hillel, who on his father's side was of Benjamin, and on his mother's side from Shefatyah son of Avital, David's wife; see there. A mother's family is not called a family [for this purpose].

(b) Rav was both his brother's son and his sister's son. He had four brothers; see Abba bar Acha above. His wife, Yehudit, bore him two sons, Yehudah and Chizkiyah, twins; see Kiddushin, chapter 1, 12b, beginning. One was delayed three months after the other. She also bore twin sisters, Pazi and Tavi. She suffered in childbirth, changed her clothing, and came before R. Chiyya. She asked, “Is a woman commanded concerning procreation?” He answered, “No.” She went and drank a sterilizing potion. Eventually the matter became known. He said, “Would that”—that is, would that you had not drunk it—“you would bear one more pregnancy of two sons”: Yevamot 65b. Shalshelet HaKabbalah, 32b, writes that the aforementioned sons married two twin sisters. It gave false testimony, for this is not found. Its mistake arose from Yevamot there: “Yehudah and Chizkiyah were brothers; Pazi and Tavi were sisters.” It understood that “Pazi and Tavi were sisters” meant the wives of Yehudah and Chizkiyah. Understand this. R. Chiyya and his sons were the equal of the Patriarchs. In Bava Metzia 85, Rabbi decreed a fast and brought R. Chiyya and his sons down before the congregation. They said “Who makes the wind blow,” and wind blew; they said “Who brings down rain,” and rain came. As they reached “Who revives the dead,” the world shook. In heaven they asked, “Who revealed the secret to the world”—that these three were esteemed like the Patriarchs? They said, “Elijah.” They brought Elijah and struck him with sixty fiery lashes. He came, appeared to them as a fiery bear, went among them, and distracted them; see there. Chullin 86a: after R. Chiyya and his sons came up, meteors, winds, and thunder ceased, and their wine did not sour; see Rashi there and Ravin bar Abba above [the source reads נר אבא]. In his days a young reem came up to the Land of Israel. It uprooted all the trees. They decreed a fast, R. Chiyya prayed, the young animal's mother lowed from the wilderness, and it went down at her call: Bereshit Rabbah, portion Noach, section 31. His wife would distress him, yet whenever he found something suitable for her he brought it to her. Rav said, “But she distresses the Master!” He replied, “It is enough for us that they raise our children and save us from sin”: Yevamot 63a, near the end. He told his wife, “Give bread to the poor promptly, so that they will give promptly to your children”: Shabbat 151b.

(c) In Shabbat 60b, R. Chiyya said: “Were it not that they would call me ‘a Babylonian who permits prohibitions’ ...” Rashi explains that R. Chiyya was Babylonian, as we say in Sukkah, “R. Chiyya and his sons came up.” Bar Kappara called him “Babylonian”: Keritot 8a; see R. Oshaya above. In Eruvin 80a, R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi said to R. Chiyya, “Babylonian.” In Ketubot, chapter 1, 5a, a Babylonian named Achiya replied. He challenged Bar Kappara with the verse, “His hands formed the dry land.” Yuchasin, letter alef, writes: “Achiya—I think this is R. Chiyya, whom Rabbi called Achiya in Moed Katan.” The reading before us is that he called him Ayya; and in Ketubot the reading before us is “and his name was R. Chiyya.” He pronounced chet as he: Megillah 24b. Rabbi called him Ayya, as did Bar Kappara (see R. Oshaya Rabbah above), disparagingly, because he could not pronounce chet. Ayin and he interchange within the guttural group alef-chet-he-ayin.

(d) In one respect he was a tanna: Bava Metzia 5a, “R. Chiyya is a tanna and may disagree.” In another he was an amora, as Rashi says in HaMappelet, Niddah 26a, that he was a tanna and an amora. He and R. Oshaya Rabbah made toseftot: Rambam's introduction to Zeraim, and Yuchasin. R. Yitzchak Abravanel, in the introduction to Nachalat Avot, says R. Chiyya composed the Tosefta; see above. Sefer Keritot, part 4, writes that R. Chiyya's Mishnah and the toseftot are two different things. Halikhot Olam writes that an anonymous Tosefta is R. Nechemyah's. In Raavad's account of tradition, Bar Kappara wrote the toseftot; R. Chiyya, R. Oshaya, and R. Shimon his colleague composed the baraitot. Tzeidah LaDerekh also writes this in its introduction; see Rabbi and R. Oshaya above. The mishnayot existed before Rabbi, who arranged them; but R. Chiyya taught as baraitot what Rabbi added to the mishnayot. R. Chiyya was Rabbi's student: Rashi, Niddah 14b. Tosafot writes that he first studied in Babylonia and came up in old age to learn from Rabbi. In old age he was Rabbi's student-colleague: he said to Rabbi, “You too did so,” without saying “you, my teacher.” Likewise Bava Batra 158b says Ben Azzai was R. Akiva's student-colleague because he said “You sit,” without saying “the Master.” Rabbi applied to him, “From a distant land, the man of my counsel”: Menachot 88b. Beer Sheva, chapter 3 of Horayot, 11b, writes that this is why Rabbi questioned R. Chiyya. Rabbi knew thirteen approaches to the Mishnah, fell ill, and forgot them. R. Chiyya restored seven approaches to him, and he recovered the other six from a launderer and restored them to Rabbi, as in Nedarim; see R. Yehudah HaNasi. His livelihood came from Rabbi. R. Shimon son of Rabbi did not resent him, out of great affection, when he took five fish and R. Shimon two: chapter Ein Tzadin, 28a. In HaNose, Ketubot 103b, when R. Chanina bar Chama and R. Chiyya disputed, R. Chanina said: “Do you dispute with me? If, Heaven forbid, Torah were forgotten from Israel, I would restore it through my reasoning.” R. Chiyya replied: “I act so that it will not be forgotten, etc.” This is what Rabbi meant by “How great are Chiyya's deeds!” See Jerusalem Megillah, chapter 4, halakhah 1. R. Shimon son of Rabbi said, “Even greater than yours?” He answered, “Yes.” R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi said, “Even greater than my father's?” He answered, “Heaven forbid! Let there be no such thing in Israel.” See Bava Metzia 85b. In Bereshit Rabbah, section 33, R. Chiyya Rabbah once entered Rabbi's presence and said, “Rav Huna is outside.” Rabbi's face changed color; see there. Rabbi told R. Chiyya, “Go out and see who wants you outside.” He went out and found no one. Realizing Rabbi was angry with him, he observed a reprimand for thirty days and did not enter Rabbi's presence. During those thirty days Rav learned from R. Chiyya all the rules of the [Torah] sections, etc. So too Jerusalem Kilayim, chapter 9, with some variation in wording. After thirty days Elijah came in R. Chiyya's likeness, put his hand on Rabbi's tooth, and it healed. When R. Chiyya came before Rabbi, he asked him, “What did you do about your tooth?” He said, “It has been healed since the moment you put your hand on it.” He replied, “I know nothing of it”—for I did not put my hand on it. Hearing this and realizing that Elijah had acted in R. Chiyya's honor, Rabbi began honoring R. Chiyya. When R. Chiyya sat before him, R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi said, “Even ahead of me?” He replied, “Heaven forbid.” There too: Rabbi was praising R. Chiyya before R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi as a great and holy man. Once R. Yishmael saw R. Chiyya in the bathhouse, and R. Chiyya did not rise for him. R. Yishmael said, “That student you praised did not rise before me.” Rabbi asked R. Chiyya why he had not risen for him. He said, “I was thinking about the aggadot of Psalms; because of my concentration, I did not see him.” Upon hearing this, Rabbi assigned him two students to enter with him. Once R. Chiyya taught his two nephews in the marketplace; Rabbi was angry with him and called him Ayya. He observed the reprimand for thirty days; see there. Jerusalem Berakhot, chapter 1, mishnah 8, and Sukkah, chapter 5, halakhah 4, relate that he demonstrated a kiddah bow before Rabbi, became lame, and recovered; see Levi. In Chullin 85b, a pest attacked his flax, and he asked Rabbi whether to slaughter a bird to treat the flax with its blood. See Rav above: this happened to Rav, who asked R. Chiyya. He expounded in Rav's name, and they praised him; in the name of “the many,” and they did not praise him: end of Mi SheAchazo.

(e) The Angel of Death could not approach R. Chiyya. He disguised himself as a poor man and knocked at the door. R. Chiyya said, “Bring out bread for the poor man.” They brought it out. He said, “The Master has mercy on a poor man; does the Master not have mercy on that man? Give me your soul, and do not trouble me to come many times.” The Angel of Death showed him a fiery whip and revealed that he was the Angel of Death. R. Chiyya made himself available to him: Moed Katan 28a, near the end. There, 25b: when R. Chiyya died, fiery stones descended from heaven. Ketubot 103b does not decide whether R. Chiyya died before Rabbi or Rabbi before R. Chiyya. In Kohelet Rabbah, on “Whatever your hand finds to do, do,” Resh Lakish—or some say R. Yehoshua ben Levi—longed to see R. Chiyya Rabbah. They told him, “You are not worthy, for you did not teach Torah as he did; moreover, he would travel to teach.” He observed three hundred fasts, and R. Chiyya appeared to him in a dream, etc. In Jerusalem Kilayim, end of chapter 9, halakhah 4, he fasted three hundred fasts without success. One must therefore say he fasted another three hundred: so Mattenot Kehunah writes. R. Assi fasted thirty days—the Jerusalem Talmud reads eighty—to see R. Chiyya Rabbah, but did not see him. They told him, “You are not worthy.” He said, “Let me see him, whatever may happen.” He saw his steps, and his eyes grew dim. Should you say that R. Assi was not a great man: a certain weaver came before R. Yochanan and said, “In a dream I saw the firmament fall, and one of your students”—R. Assi, see there—“supported it with his hand.” Bava Metzia 85b: R. Zeira said, “R. Yosi son of R. Chanina appeared to me in a dream. I asked him, ‘Beside whom are you stationed’”—sitting in the heavenly academy? “He said, ‘Beside R. Yochanan.’ ‘And R. Yochanan beside whom?’ ‘Beside R. Yannai.’ ‘And R. Yannai beside whom?’ ‘Beside R. Chanina.’ ‘And R. Chanina beside whom?’ ‘Beside R. Chiyya.’ I asked, ‘And R. Yochanan is not beside R. Chiyya?’”—is R. Yochanan not worthy to sit beside R. Chiyya? “He said, ‘Where there are fiery sparks and burning flames, who brings the smith's son there?’” R. Yochanan is called Bar Nappacha, “the smith's son” (see there), hence “Who brings the smith's son there?” There too, R. Chaviva said: “Rav Chaviva bar Surmaki told me: I saw a certain scholar whom Elijah visited regularly. In the morning his eyes were fine, but in the evening they looked burned by fire. I asked what had happened. He told me: ‘I asked Elijah to show me the rabbis as they ascend to the heavenly academy. He told me, “You may look at all of them, except R. Chiyya's palanquin: do not look at it.” “What is their distinguishing sign?” “Angels accompany all of them as they ascend and descend; R. Chiyya's palanquin ascends and descends by itself.” I could not restrain myself and looked at it. Two fiery sparks came and struck him and blinded his eyes. The next day I went and prostrated myself at his cave, saying, “I study the Master's baraitot,” and was healed.’” The parenthetical explanation says: “I constantly study my master's Tosefta, which he arranged in six orders.” R. Chiyya arranged them, as we say elsewhere: “If Rabbi did not teach it, where did R. Chiyya get it?”—Eruvin 92a; Niddah 62b. We also say: “Do not raise an objection in the study house from any baraita not taught in the schools of R. Chiyya and R. Oshaya”; see there. End of Rashi's words. Gilgulei Neshamot, letter yod, writes that Jesse entered R. Chiyya through soul impregnation. This explains the story in chapter Asarah Yuchasin of R. Chiyya soliciting his maidservant: his wife was certainly an impregnation of the soul of the wife of Jesse, David's father. The children repeat their fathers' deeds, for he would direct his intention to this cup while drinking from another. When Jesse grew angry with his wife and solicited his maidservant, she told her mistress, who secretly went to her husband. Jesse thought he was having intercourse with his maidservant. David therefore said, “In iniquity I was brought forth,” for David was born from that union. As for Jesse's dying through the serpent's counsel: the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join an evil thought to an act. Rather, He brought him through soul impregnation into R. Chiyya, whose abundant merit would confer merit on Jesse. His great power is known: when he prayed, rain came; when he said “Who revives the dead,” the world shook. They said, “You may look at all the palanquins except R. Chiyya's.” End of quotation. This requires investigation: neither chapter Asarah Yuchasin nor anywhere in the Talmud has such a story about R. Chiyya the Great. Such an event happened to R. Chiyya bar Ashi. I did not wish to intervene and place it there, because perhaps the writer found an aggadah in which this also happened to R. Chiyya the Great, and mistakenly wrote that it was in Asarah Yuchasin. Gelilot Eretz Yisrael writes that R. Chiyya and his sons Yehudah and Chizkiyah are buried in the cemetery at Tiberias opposite the city gate. Benjamin's Travels places the tombs of our holy Rabbi, R. Chiyya from Babylonia, and Yonah ben Amittai at Tzippori, at the top of the mountain.

(f) R. Abba bar Zutra, in his name. R. Avin, in his name. R. Acha bar Avya; and R. Oshaya Berabbi, whose daughter-in-law came before R. Chiyya (see there). Rav Oshaya bar Chiyya (see there). Rav Achai (see there). Bar Yoshiyah asked him. Achi taught in his house and asked him. Aivu, his brother. R. Elazar, his student. R. Bisna, in his name. R. Bivi bar Avin, in his name. R. Huna, R. Chelbo, and Rav, in his name: Shekalim, chapter 1. Rav Chunah Rabbah, in his name. Chizkiyah, his son. Rav Chana, his brother. R. Chanina, in his name; see above. And Chalfa bar Idi. Rav Yehudah, in his name. Yehudah, his son. Yochanan Chakoka; and R. Yonatan (see above). R. Yonatan ben Yosef. “Rav Yosef said: R. Chiyya said.” Abba Yosi HaTorati; and R. Yannai—Jerusalem Berakhot, chapter 4, mishnah 5. R. Yannai, his student. R. Yirmeyah, in his name. R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi said to him. Marta, his brother. In the name of R. Paddai. Rav, his student. Rabbah bar bar Chana, his student. “Rabbah said: R. Chiyya said”—Shabbat 127a; Eruvin 78a, 88a. Rabbi, his teacher; or he was Rabbi's student-colleague (see above). R. Shabbetai, in his name. Shila, his brother. Shmuel, in his name—Shabbat 45b, near the end, 138a, near the end; Sukkah 11a, near the end; Chullin 113a, 138a. Shimon son of Rabbi: Yuchasin writes that he was his teacher. See there, where I wrote in Tosafot's name that he was greater than R. Chiyya. But since Tosafot writes that in old age R. Chiyya was Rabbi's student-colleague, how could he be the student of R. Shimon son of Rabbi? R. Shimon ben Lakish, in his name—Avodah Zarah 30a. In the name of R. Shimon ben Elazar—Ruth Rabbah, beginning. He went with R. Yonatan before the bier of R. Shimon ben Yosi ben Lekunya—Jerusalem Berakhot. He said to R. Shimon ben Chalafta Berabbi—Jerusalem Berakhot, chapter 1, passage 1, and beginning of Amar Lahem HaMemunneh. Rav Sheshet, in his name.
